response.title: Can I leave a power station and solar panels at my cabin all winter, or will the cold ruin the battery?
response.answer:
Yes, you can leave solar panels and a portable power station at your cabin all winter, but the battery needs special attention. Cold weather usually won't permanently damage a lithium battery by itself. The biggest danger is charging the battery when it's below freezing.

The answer depends on your power station's battery chemistry, how cold your cabin gets, and whether you plan to leave the solar panels connected.

What happens in freezing temperatures?

Temperature

	

Lithium power station

	

Solar panels




32°F to 50°F (0–10°C)

	

Generally safe; charging may be limited

	

Safe




0°F to 32°F (−18–0°C)

	

Storage often OK; charging can be dangerous

	

Safe




−20°F to 0°F (−29 to −18°C)

	

May exceed storage limits

	

Generally safe




Below −20°F (−29°C)

	

Higher risk; check manufacturer limits

	

Usually safe if rated

These are general guidelines, not universal manufacturer specifications.

Most modern power stations use LiFePO4 (LFP) batteries, which are relatively durable. However:

Cold storage: Usually acceptable within the manufacturer's specified storage range.

Cold discharge: Often possible below freezing, although usable capacity and output can decrease.

Cold charging: Typically prohibited below 32°F (0°C) unless the unit has an approved battery-heating or low-temperature charging system.

Charging LiFePO4 cells below their permitted temperature can cause lithium plating, permanently reducing battery capacity and potentially creating a safety risk.

What I recommend for your cabin

Solar panels: Leave them outside.

Rigid outdoor-rated panels generally handle freezing temperatures well. Secure them against wind and snow loads, and protect cables and connectors from moisture. Snow covering the panels will reduce production.

Power station: Store it disconnected if unused.

For winter storage, follow the manufacturer's recommended charge level (often around 50–80%), turn it off, and disconnect the solar input. Check whether the manufacturer requires periodic recharging. Avoid leaving it for months below its rated storage temperature.

If you want the solar panels to keep the power station charged automatically throughout winter, that's a different situation. You'll need a power station with reliable low-temperature charging protection, ideally a built-in battery heater. Some EcoFlow systems support automatic battery heating, but not every model does. 
EcoFlow US
+2

Two questions that will determine whether your setup is safe

What brand and model is your power station? (EcoFlow DELTA 2, Jackery Explorer 1000, Bluetti AC200, etc.)

How cold does your cabin get in winter? For example, 20°F, 0°F, or −20°F?

With those two details, I can tell you whether you can safely leave everything connected all winter or should disconnect and store the battery differently.
